month.title: Automation + tool use
month.theme: Connect systems carefully: automations that are observable, reversible and human-reviewed.
month.mastery: Design a workflow that handles failures instead of assuming everything succeeds.
month.checkpoint: One useful workflow running end to end, with logs, retries, an approval step and a tested failure path.

weeks.title: Workflow mapping
weeks.objective: See a workflow clearly before automating it (who does what, when, with which data) and where it breaks.
learn: The happy path vs exception paths
Where judgment is needed (keep humans there)
Data that flows between systems, and how sensitive it is
practice: Map your own weekly invoicing, file-delivery or content workflow
Time each step during one real run
Mark every step that can fail, and what happens then
Interview one person about a workflow they hate

build.title: Workflow map + automation brief
build.brief: Map one real recurring workflow (yours, or someone you know) as a swimlane diagram including exceptions, and write an automation brief: what to automate, what stays human, and the success measure.

weeks.prove: Walk the person who owns the workflow through your map and get at least two corrections.
reflect: Which step looked automatable until you mapped its exceptions?
weeks.ship: The map and brief in your repo (or a FigJam link).

tryFirst.task: A studio's client onboarding goes: enquiry form, call, proposal, advance invoice, kickoff folder. Which steps would you automate first, and which would you never automate?
tryFirst.hint: Score each step on frequency, time cost, error risk, and how much judgment it needs.
tryFirst.explanation: Automate high-frequency, low-judgment, rule-based steps first (creating folders, sending templated invoices). Keep humans on judgment-heavy relationship steps (the call, scoping the proposal). Add AI only where it removes drudgery without removing accountability.
tryFirst.solution:
Automate first:   enquiry -> CRM row + acknowledgement email; paid invoice -> kickoff folder + checklist
Assist, don't automate:   proposal draft from call notes (AI draft, human edits)
Never automate:   the discovery call; pricing decisions
Measure:   hours per week saved, errors caught, time to kickoff

weeks.title: Webhooks + APIs
weeks.objective: Let systems notify each other reliably, and handle the messy reality of events.
learn: Webhook payloads and signatures (verifying the sender)
practice: Receive a webhook from GitHub or a forms tool into a local endpoint through a tunnel
Replay the same event twice, and make the second one a no-op
Store raw events before processing them

build.title: Webhook receiver
build.brief: An endpoint that receives events from a real service (GitHub, a payment provider in test mode, a forms tool), verifies them, stores them, processes them idempotently, and shows an event log page.

weeks.prove: Send a duplicate, a forged (unsigned) and a malformed event. Show the log handling each one correctly.
reflect: Which assumption about events turned out to be false?
weeks.ship: Webhook receiver on GitHub with an event-handling diagram.

tryFirst.task: Your webhook handler sometimes receives the same 'payment.captured' event twice and records two payments. Fix it.
tryFirst.hint: Every event has an id. What if you remembered which ids you've already processed, enforced by the database?
tryFirst.explanation: Treat event delivery as 'at least once'. Store the event id with a UNIQUE constraint; if the insert conflicts, you've seen it already, so acknowledge it and skip.

weeks.title: Automation tools such as n8n
weeks.objective: Build useful automations quickly with a workflow tool, and know when to drop down to code.
learn: Credentials and secrets in automation tools
practice: Complete the n8n Level One course
Build: form, validate, Google Sheet, email
Add an error workflow that notifies you
Rebuild one step as a small code function

build.title: n8n workflow for your mapped process
build.brief: Implement your Week 33 automation brief in n8n (or a similar tool): trigger, validation, the main steps, an approval step, error notification and a run log.

weeks.prove: Break it on purpose in three ways (bad input, downstream outage, duplicate trigger) and show it recovering or alerting.
reflect: Where did the no-code tool help, and where did it get in your way?
weeks.ship: Exported workflow JSON, screenshots and a README in your repo.

tryFirst.task: Your n8n workflow posts to a client's Slack. If Slack is down, the run fails silently. Make failure visible and recoverable.
tryFirst.hint: Workflow tools can run a separate workflow when one fails. And a failed step can be retried before giving up.
tryFirst.explanation: Set retries with a wait on the flaky node, then an error workflow that alerts you with the run id and payload so you can re-run it manually. Silent failure is the real bug.
tryFirst.solution:
1. Slack node -> Settings -> Retry On Fail: 3 tries, wait 5 seconds.
2. Workflow settings -> Error Workflow: 'Alert me'.
3. 'Alert me' = Error Trigger -> email or Telegram with the workflow name, failed node and execution URL.
4. Keep the original payload in a sheet or database so a manual re-run is possible.

weeks.title: AI tool calling / agents
weeks.objective: Let a model take actions through tools, with tight permissions, approvals and an audit trail.
learn: Tool calling: the model proposes, your code executes
Read vs write tools; least privilege
The agent loop, and why to keep it short
practice: Give a model one read-only tool and watch the calls it makes
Validate tool arguments with a schema
Add a confirmation step before a write tool runs
Make a tool fail and see how the model reacts

build.title: AI step with tools in your workflow
build.brief: Add an AI step to your automation that uses one read tool and one write tool (for example: look up a client, draft a follow-up), with schema validation, approval before any write, and a log of every call.

weeks.prove: Mastery test: design a workflow that handles failures instead of assuming everything succeeds.
reflect: What would happen if the model called your write tool with the wrong arguments?
weeks.ship: Workflow with AI tool use, plus an architecture diagram and log screenshots.

tryFirst.task: A model wants to call send_email({ to, subject, body }). Design the execution code so this can never send an email the user didn't approve.
tryFirst.hint: The model only proposes. Your code decides whether, when, and with what arguments the tool actually runs.
tryFirst.explanation: Validate the arguments, check them against policy (allowed recipients), then require explicit human approval for anything with side effects. Log the proposal, the decision and the result.

mastery.title: A workflow that handles failure
mastery.challenge: Run your automated workflow end to end and prove it behaves correctly when things go wrong, not just when they go right.
constraints: A real workflow (yours or a willing person's), with test or permissioned data
Any tool or code, but every failure path must be designed, not accidental
criteria: A failure map: each step's failure mode and its designed response
A duplicate trigger is handled idempotently
A downstream outage leads to retry, then alert, then a manual recovery path
Invalid input is rejected with a useful message
Every run (and every tool call, if AI is used) is logged and inspectable
Demonstrated live or recorded: three induced failures, three correct recoveries
